themes.name: High sensitivity screening models
themes.description: Studies reporting LLMs achieving sensitivity of roughly 90% or higher for title/abstract or full‑text screening, indicating strong ability to identify relevant records.

themes.name: Ensemble and prompt‑optimization approaches
themes.description: Studies that improve performance through prompt engineering, model ensembles, full‑agreement strategies, or calibrated zero‑shot ensembles.

themes.name: Fine‑tuned or specialized LLMs
themes.description: Studies evaluating fine‑tuned, domain‑specific, or compact LLMs and comparing them with general‑purpose models for systematic review screening.

themes.name: Other findings
themes.description: Studies not covered by the themes above.

High sensitivity screening models.narrative: High‑sensitivity screening models using large language models (LLMs) consistently report sensitivities at or above 90% for title and abstract screening. Li et al. found GPT‑4 achieved 90% average sensitivity across 3,715 abstracts, with 97% in one set and 90% in another, though specificity varied widely (59%–93%) [R0011]. Oami et al. showed that after prompt modification GPT‑4 Turbo reached 0.91 sensitivity (95% CI 0.77‑0.97) while maintaining 0.98 specificity on 16,669 records, highlighting the impact of prompt engineering [R0010]. Qiu et al. reported three independent datasets where the LLM attained 98%–100% sensitivity for abstract screening, with specificity ranging from 80.6% to 93% [R0079]. Zhan et al. observed 99.2% sensitivity for title/abstract screening across four systematic reviews, albeit with lower specificity (83.6%) [R0049]. In contrast, López‑Pineda et al. reported lower sensitivities (77.5% for Llama 3 and 56.2% for ChatGPT‑4o mini) despite high specificities, suggesting model version and prompting affect performance [R0037]. Nordmann et al. achieved 88%–89% sensitivity on 15,307 abstracts with a dual‑reviewer reference standard, illustrating that even large samples can yield sub‑90% sensitivity when the LLM or workflow differs [R0073]. Across studies, higher sensitivities are associated with larger LLMs (GPT‑4 variants), refined prompts, and fine‑tuning, whereas variability stems from differing reference standards, sample sizes, and reporting completeness.
High sensitivity screening models.certainty_rationale: Evidence is primarily from diagnostic accuracy studies with some concerns for bias and inconsistency across models, prompts, and reference standards, leading to downgrades for risk of bias and inconsistency.

Ensemble and prompt‑optimization approac.narrative: Ensemble and prompt‑optimization strategies consistently improve LLM screening accuracy compared with single‑model baselines. In Oami et al., modifying the prompt raised integrated sensitivity from 0.75 to 0.91 while specificity remained above 0.98, demonstrating the impact of prompt engineering on a dataset of 16,670 records [R0010]. Sanghera et al. reported that zero‑shot prompting combined with optimal prompt selection achieved up to 100% sensitivity on a balanced development set and maintained high sensitivity (0.756‑1.000) on a large 119,695‑record cohort, though precision fell markedly due to class imbalance; ensemble LLM‑human combinations restored precision to 0.1450 while preserving perfect sensitivity, highlighting the benefit of model ensembles for workload reduction [R0025]. Guo et al. found that a single GPT API with a criteria‑based prompt yielded overall accuracy of 0.91 and a macro F1 of 0.60 on 24,307 abstracts, with higher inter‑rater agreement (κ=0.96) than between two human reviewers (κ=0.46), suggesting that well‑crafted prompts can approach human consistency [R0028]. Hilkenmeier et al. showed that requiring full agreement across three distinct LLMs produced precision 0.88, recall 0.96, and F1 0.92, outperforming prior single‑LLM results, indicating that consensus ensembles mitigate individual model errors [R0061]. Wang et al. confirmed that calibrated zero‑shot ensembles outperformed individual generative LLMs, emphasizing the role of calibration and ensemble weighting for higher work‑saved‑screening and precision [R0138]. Across studies, higher sensitivity often coincided with lower precision when class imbalance was extreme, and variability in performance appears linked to LLM version, dataset size, and prompt design. Risk of bias was generally rated as some concerns, and several reports lacked full sample details, tempering confidence in the magnitude of gains.
Ensemble and prompt‑optimization approac.certainty_rationale: Evidence is observational with some risk of bias and inconsistency across datasets and prompting methods, leading to downgrades for risk of bias and inconsistency.

Fine‑tuned or specialized LLMs.narrative: Fine‑tuned, domain‑specific LLMs appear to outperform general‑purpose models and non‑expert humans in abstract screening. In a retinal vasculitis review, the fine‑tuned UveAItis model achieved 93.3% accuracy, an AUC of 0.887, sensitivity of 81.7% and specificity of 95.7%, exceeding GPT‑4o (AUC 0.805) and Claude Sonnet 3.5 (AUC 0.669) [R0069]. A larger 8,277‑record dataset showed that full‑parameter fine‑tuning of a 1.2 B‑parameter LLM raised weighted F1 by 80.79% and yielded 86.4% overall agreement with a single human coder, with sensitivity 91.18% and specificity 86.38% [R0096]. Compact models applied with structured prompts across three systematic reviews (including datasets of 7,693 and 21,116 records) reached up to 100% sensitivity but low precision (<10%); balanced accuracy ranged from 76.7% to 91.3% and the best model attained specificity of 92.7% [R0072]. In a scoping review of 15,307 abstracts, ChatGPT‑4.0 achieved 68% accuracy, sensitivity around 88–89% and specificity 67%, delivering a 64% workload saving while still requiring human oversight [R0073]. A validation of GPT‑4 with chain‑of‑thought prompting reported 71% sensitivity, 89% specificity and 84% overall accuracy compared with consensus human decisions [R0145]. Across studies, performance varied with model size, fine‑tuning strategy, and reviewer workflow, and risk‑of‑bias concerns (e.g., lack of blinding, unclear confounding control) temper confidence in the estimates.
Fine‑tuned or specialized LLMs.certainty_rationale: Evidence is downgraded from high due to moderate risk of bias in several studies and inconsistency in performance metrics across models and datasets.

Other findings.narrative: In a prospective diagnostic study, LLM‑assisted title and abstract screening achieved a pooled sensitivity of 0.73 (95% CI 0.57‑0.85) and a specificity of 0.99 (95% CI 0.97‑0.99), yielding an AUC of 0.97 (95% CI 0.96‑0.99) when compared with dual independent human reviewers as the reference standard [R0018]. Post‑hoc prompt revisions markedly improved sensitivity to 0.98 (95% CI 0.74‑1.00) while preserving high specificity (0.98, 95% CI 0.94‑0.99), indicating that prompt engineering can substantially affect performance [R0018]. For full‑text screening, the same LLMs showed sensitivity of 0.87 (95% CI 0.77‑0.99) and specificity of 0.96 (95% CI 0.91‑0.98), with an AUC of 0.96 (95% CI 0.94‑0.97), suggesting comparable accuracy to manual screening across both stages [R0018]. The study also reported that LLMs outperformed traditional machine‑learning tools such as ASReview (sensitivity 0.58) and Abstrackr (sensitivity 0.48), highlighting a potential advantage of large language models over earlier algorithms [R0018]. However, the authors noted a key limitation: the use of previously published systematic reviews may overlap with LLM training data, introducing selection bias and possibly inflating performance estimates [R0018]. The evidence rests on a single full‑text report with some concerns for bias, and sample size details were not provided, limiting precision.
Other findings.certainty_rationale: Observational diagnostic design with some risk of bias (training data overlap) and imprecision due to missing sample size; inconsistency not evident but indirectness and bias lead to downgrading.

discussion.summary_of_evidence: Across 21 diagnostic accuracy studies, large language models (LLMs) generally achieved high sensitivity for title and abstract screening, often exceeding 90% when using the most advanced models (e.g., GPT‑4 variants) and optimized prompts [R0011,R0010,R0079,R0049]. Sensitivity tended to be lower for earlier or smaller models such as Llama 3 and ChatGPT‑4o mini, highlighting the influence of model version and prompting [R0037,R0073]. Ensemble and prompt‑optimization approaches consistently boosted performance, raising sensitivity to 0.91–1.00 while maintaining specificity above 0.95 in several large datasets, though precision sometimes declined with extreme class imbalance [R0010,R0025,R0028,R0061,R0138]. Fine‑tuned, domain‑specific LLMs outperformed general‑purpose counterparts, achieving accuracies around 93%, sensitivities of 81–91% and specificities up to 96% [R0069,R0096,R0072]. A single prospective study reported pooled sensitivity of 0.73 and specificity of 0.99, with post‑hoc prompt revisions improving sensitivity to 0.98, suggesting that prompt engineering can markedly affect outcomes [R0018]. Overall, the evidence is of moderate certainty due to some concerns about bias, inconsistency across models and reference standards, and occasional incomplete reporting.
discussion.limitations_of_evidence: Most studies were observational diagnostic accuracy designs with some concerns for bias, including lack of blinding, unclear handling of confounding, and potential overlap between LLM training data and screened systematic reviews [R0018,R0037,R0073]. Sample sizes and reporting completeness varied widely, limiting the precision of pooled estimates. Heterogeneity in reference standards (single versus dual reviewer, consensus versus adjudication) and in prompt or fine‑tuning procedures contributed to inconsistency across findings. Few studies evaluated full‑text screening, and many relied on retrospective datasets, reducing external validity.
discussion.implications: The findings suggest that LLMs, particularly when fine‑tuned or used within ensemble and prompt‑optimized workflows, can reliably support title and abstract screening, potentially reducing reviewer workload while maintaining high sensitivity. Practitioners should adopt rigorous prompt engineering and consider ensemble strategies to balance sensitivity and precision. Future research should conduct prospective, blinded comparisons, standardize reference standards, and explore the impact of training‑data overlap. Reporting of sample characteristics, blinding procedures, and detailed performance metrics will be essential to strengthen the evidence base.

rationale: Automated title‑and‑abstract screening is widely promoted as a way to lessen the labour‑intensive workload of systematic reviews, yet the empirical evidence for large language models (LLMs) in this role remains fragmented. Several recent investigations have begun to evaluate LLMs for screening, reporting mixed accuracy and highlighting the need for systematic synthesis of comparative performance data [R0108]. Early work has demonstrated that fine‑tuned, smaller LLMs can be promising for large‑scale reviews, but these studies have been limited to single models or specific domains [R0096]. More comprehensive assessments have emerged, testing state‑of‑the‑art models such as GPT‑4 and GPT‑4o Mini against human reviewers and reporting sensitivity, specificity, and workload reductions across thousands of records and multiple clinical topics [R0045, R0028, R0072]. Nonetheless, direct head‑to‑head comparisons between LLMs and traditional supervised machine‑learning baselines are scarce, and the methodological quality of existing reports varies, making it difficult for reviewers to gauge reliability and to decide whether to adopt LLMs in practice [R0058]. A systematic review that aggregates these heterogeneous findings will clarify the current accuracy of LLM‑assisted screening, identify conditions under which LLMs approach or exceed human performance, and pinpoint gaps that future research must address.

revision_issues.description: Studies assigned to this theme are never cited in its narrative: R0073, R0145.
revision_issues.suggested_fix: Report what these studies found, or explain why they add nothing.

revision_issues.description: Unsupported statement: "Yamoah et al. achieved 88% sensitivity with a dual‑reviewer reference standard on a large sample of 15,307 abstracts [R0073]." — Wrong study cited. The sample size of 15,307 abstracts and the sensitivity of ~88-89% belong to Nordmann et al. (2026) [R0073], not Yamoah et al. (2026) [R0096]. Yamoah et al. studied a sample of 8,277 records and achieved 91.18% sensitivity.
revision_issues.suggested_fix: Change the citation to [R0073] (Nordmann et al.) or correct the author name to Nordmann et al. If referring to Yamoah et al., the sample size should be 8,277 and sensitivity 91.18%.

revision_issues.description: Unsupported statement: "Across three reviews (7,693–21,116 records), compact models using structured prompts achieved up to 100% sensitivity but low precision (<10%); balanced accuracy varied from 76.7% to 91.3% and specificity reached 92.7% for the best model [R0072]." — The evidence card for [R0072] lists only two specific record counts (21,116 for AB review and 7,693 for COVID-19 review) and states the study involved 'three systematic reviews'. It does not provide the record count for the third review, so the range '7,693–21,116' is not fully supported by the provided evidence text. Additionally, while the findings mention 'low precision below 10%', the specific value '92.7%' for specificity is listed in the 'Effects' section but not explicitly linked to 'the best model' in the narrative findings, though this is a minor interpretation. The primary issue is the unsupported range implying all three reviews fall within that specific min-max range without evidence for the third.
revision_issues.suggested_fix: Change 'Across three reviews (7,693–21,116 records)' to 'Across three reviews (including datasets of 7,693 and 21,116 records)' or simply 'Across three reviews' to avoid asserting a range that covers all three without explicit data for the third.

revision_issues.description: "Certainty of evidence was rated moderate to low." — The thematic synthesis explicitly rates the certainty as 'moderate' for all four themes. The abstract introduces a 'low' rating that is not supported by the provided synthesis.
revision_issues.suggested_fix: Change 'moderate to low' to 'moderate' to align with the certainty ratings in the synthesis.

revision_issues.description: "Fine-tuned, domain-specific LLMs demonstrated superior balanced accuracy compared with general-purpose models, achieving sensitivities around 81–91% and specificities up to 96% [R0069,R0096,R0072,R0045,R0058,R0085]." — The citation list includes R0045, R0058, and R0085, which the synthesis identifies as non-fine-tuned or general-purpose models (GPT-4 evaluation, Llama-3.1 zero-shot, GPT-4 prompt engineering). Including them in the sentence describing 'Fine-tuned' models is factually incorrect and contradicts the synthesis's distinction between fine-tuned and general-purpose performance.
revision_issues.suggested_fix: Remove R0045, R0058, and R0085 from the citation list for the fine-tuned model claim, or restructure the sentence to separate fine-tuned results from general-purpose comparisons.
